chapters.n: Paul opens his longest letter, writing from Corinth around AD 57 to saints in Rome he had never visited. He introduces himself as Christ’s servant, called as an apostle and set apart for the gospel.

f.g: Greek doulos — a bond-servant or slave; a title of humble devotion.

chapters.n: The gospel isn’t new — God promised it long ago through his prophets in scripture. Paul roots the good news in Israel’s sacred history.
The gospel is all about God’s Son, Jesus Christ. In his mortal lineage he descended from King David, as the Messiah was prophesied to.
His resurrection powerfully proclaimed him as the Son of God. Christ has two natures in view here: born of David in the flesh, and revealed as divine through rising from the dead.

f.w: by the resurrection from the dead

chapters.n: Through Christ, Paul received grace and his apostleship, with a mission to bring people of all nations to “the obedience of faith” — faith that shows itself in obedience.
The Roman saints are among those called to belong to Jesus Christ.
Paul greets all the believers in Rome as God’s beloved, called to be saints. “Grace and peace” blends a Greek greeting (grace) with the Hebrew shalom (peace).

f.g: Holy ones — all members of the Church, not just exceptional individuals.

chapters.n: Paul first gives thanks: the faith of the Roman saints was being talked about everywhere. Their example reached far beyond their city.

f.w: your faith is spoken of throughout the whole world

chapters.n: Paul calls God as witness that he constantly prays for them, though he has never met them.
He prays that, God willing, he can finally come to visit them. He did eventually arrive — as a prisoner.
He longs to see them so he can share some spiritual gift to strengthen them.
Paul humbly corrects himself: rather, so that we can encourage one another by our shared faith. Even an apostle receives strength from the members.
He wants them to know he had often planned to come but had been prevented until now. He hoped for a harvest among them as among other Gentiles.

f.g: Hindered, prevented. (In the King James era “let” could mean “hinder.”)

chapters.n: Paul feels obligated to everyone — Greeks and non-Greeks, educated and uneducated alike. Having received the gospel, he owes it to all.

f.g: To Greeks, anyone who didn’t speak Greek.

chapters.n: So he is eager to preach the gospel in Rome too.

f.w: as much as in me is
f.g: As far as it depends on me; I’m eager.

chapters.n: The letter’s theme: Paul isn’t ashamed of the gospel, because it is God’s power to save everyone who believes — first the Jews, then the Gentiles. In Rome, power was everything; Paul names the true power.

f.w: I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ
the power of God unto salvation

chapters.n: In the gospel, God reveals his righteousness — his way of making people right with him — from beginning to end by faith. Paul quotes Habakkuk: the righteous shall live by faith.

f.w: The just shall live by faith

f.g: Both God’s own justice and the gift by which he makes people right with him.

chapters.n: Paul now begins showing why everyone needs this gospel: God’s wrath is revealed against all ungodliness. People suppress the truth by their wickedness.

f.g: God’s just opposition to sin — not a temper, but his settled response to evil.
Hold down, suppress the truth by living wickedly.

chapters.n: What can be known about God is plain to them, because God has shown it.
Since creation, God’s invisible qualities — his eternal power and divine nature — have been visible through the things he made. So no one has an excuse.

f.w: being understood by the things that are made

chapters.n: Though people knew God, they didn’t honor him or thank him. Their thinking became futile and their hearts darkened. Ingratitude is the first step away from God.
Claiming to be wise, they became fools.
They traded the glory of the immortal God for idols shaped like mortal humans, birds, animals, and reptiles — echoing Israel’s golden calf.

f.w: changed the glory of the uncorruptible God

chapters.n: So God let them go their own way, handing them over to the impure desires of their hearts. Part of God’s judgment is allowing people to experience the consequences they choose.

f.g: God handed them over — let them follow their chosen path.

chapters.n: They exchanged God’s truth for a lie, worshipping created things instead of the Creator. Paul breaks into praise: the Creator is blessed forever!

f.w: the creature more than the Creator
f.g: Created things rather than the one who created them.

chapters.n: Because of this, God gave them up to dishonorable passions. Paul gives the example of women exchanging natural relations for unnatural ones.

Likewise men abandoned natural relations with women and burned with desire for one another, reaping the consequences of their error. Paul presents this as one example among many of how humanity has turned from God’s design.
Because they didn’t see fit to keep God in their awareness, God gave them over to a corrupted mind, doing what should not be done.

f.g: Rejected, failing the test — unfit for good judgment.

chapters.n: Paul lists sins that fill a godless society: injustice, immorality, greed, malice, envy, murder, strife, deceit, ill will, and gossip.
The list continues: slanderers, God-haters, the insolent, arrogant, boastful, inventors of new evils, and children who disobey parents.
And more: senseless, faithless, heartless, unforgiving, and merciless.
Worst of all, they know God’s judgment that such things deserve death, yet they not only do them but applaud others who do. Celebrating sin is a further step into darkness.

f.w: have pleasure in them that do them

chapters.n: Paul now turns to the reader who nodded along at chapter 1’s list of sins. If you condemn others for these things while doing them yourself, you condemn yourself.

f.w: wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself

chapters.n: We know God’s judgment is always based on truth — he judges fairly and accurately.
Do you really think you’ll escape God’s judgment when you do the same things you condemn in others?
Or do you take God’s kindness, patience, and long-suffering for granted? His goodness is meant to lead you to repent — not to make you comfortable in sin.

f.w: the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance

chapters.n: A stubborn, unrepentant heart is like storing up treasure — except what you’re saving is wrath for the day God’s just judgment is revealed.
God will repay each person according to what they have done.
To those who patiently keep doing good, seeking glory, honor, and immortality, God will give eternal life.
But for those who are self-seeking, reject the truth, and follow wickedness, there will be anger and wrath.
Trouble and distress will come to everyone who does evil — the Jew first and also the Gentile. Privileged position brings greater accountability.
But glory, honor, and peace will come to everyone who does good — Jew first and also Gentile.
God shows no favoritism. He judges everyone by the same just standard.

f.w: there is no respect of persons with God

chapters.n: Those who sinned without having the law of Moses will be judged without it; those who had the law will be judged by it. God judges people by the light they had.
It isn’t hearing the law that makes someone righteous before God, but doing it.

f.w: not the hearers of the law are just before God, but the doers

chapters.n: When Gentiles without the law of Moses naturally do what it requires, they show they have an inner law of their own.
They show that God’s law is written on their hearts. Their conscience testifies, and their thoughts accuse or defend them. Latter-day Saints connect this to the Light of Christ given to everyone.
All this will be revealed on the day when God judges people’s hidden secrets through Jesus Christ, as Paul’s gospel teaches.
Paul now addresses the Jewish reader directly: you bear the name of Jew, rely on the law, and boast in your relationship with God.

f.g: Rely on, lean on the law.

chapters.n: You know God’s will and can recognize what is best, because you were taught from the law.
You are confident you are a guide for the blind and a light for those in darkness — Israel’s calling indeed.

f.w: a light of them which are in darkness

chapters.n: You see yourself as a teacher of the foolish and the young, since the law gives you the very form of knowledge and truth.
So — you who teach others, do you teach yourself? You preach against stealing; do you steal?
You condemn adultery; do you commit it? You despise idols; do you rob temples? Hypocrisy undercuts every sermon.

f.g: Robbing temples — perhaps profiting from pagan shrines while condemning idols.

chapters.n: You boast in the law but dishonor God by breaking it.
As scripture says, God’s name is mocked among the Gentiles because of the behavior of his people. Our conduct reflects on God.

f.w: the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles through you

chapters.n: Circumcision has real value if you keep the law; but if you break it, your circumcision becomes meaningless. Outward signs need inward obedience.

f.g: The covenant sign given to Abraham and his descendants.

chapters.n: If an uncircumcised Gentile keeps the law’s righteous requirements, won’t God count him as though he were circumcised?
In fact, the law-keeping Gentile will stand as a witness against the Jew who has the written law and circumcision but breaks the law.
Being a true Jew isn’t a matter of outward appearance, and true circumcision isn’t merely physical.

f.w: he is not a Jew, which is one outwardly

chapters.n: A true Jew is one inwardly, and real circumcision is of the heart — by the Spirit, not just the written code. Such a person seeks God’s approval, not people’s. (“Jew” comes from Judah, meaning “praise.”)

f.w: circumcision is that of the heart
whose praise is not of men, but of God
f.g: A wordplay: “Judah” sounds like the Hebrew for “praise” (Genesis 29:35).

chapters.n: Paul anticipates an objection: if being a “real Jew” is inward, is there any advantage to being Jewish or circumcised at all?
Yes, much! Above all, the Jews were entrusted with God’s revelations — the scriptures. That was a priceless stewardship.

f.g: God’s spoken words — the revealed scriptures.

f.w: unto them were committed the oracles of God

chapters.n: What if some were unfaithful? Does their unfaithfulness cancel God’s faithfulness? Paul asks whether human failure can break God’s promises.

f.g: God’s faithfulness, his reliability in keeping promises.

chapters.n: Absolutely not! God stays true even if every person proves false. Paul quotes David’s psalm of repentance: God is right when he speaks and wins when he is judged.

f.g: Greek mē genoito — “May it never be!” — Paul’s strongest denial.

f.w: That thou mightest be justified in thy sayings

chapters.n: Another objection: if our wrongdoing makes God’s righteousness shine brighter, isn’t God unfair to punish us? Paul admits he is voicing a human argument.

f.g: I’m using a human way of reasoning.

chapters.n: Of course not — otherwise how could God judge the world at all?

f.w: how shall God judge the world?

chapters.n: The objector presses: if my lie ends up glorifying God by contrast, why am I still judged as a sinner?
Some critics even claimed Paul taught, “Let’s do evil so good may come.” Paul calls this a slander, and says those who reason that way deserve condemnation.
So are we Jews better off morally? Not at all. Paul has already shown that Jews and Gentiles alike are all under the power of sin.
Paul strings together Old Testament verses, starting with: “There is none righteous, no, not one.” No one can claim to be sinless on their own.

f.w: There is none righteous, no, not one

chapters.n: No one truly understands or seeks God on their own.

f.w: there is none that seeketh after God

chapters.n: All have turned aside and become worthless together; no one does good, not even one.

f.g: Useless, gone bad — like spoiled milk.

chapters.n: The quotations now describe sinful speech: throats like open graves, tongues that deceive, lips with snake venom.

f.w: Their throat is an open sepulchre
the poison of asps is under their lips

chapters.n: Their mouths are full of cursing and bitterness.

f.w: Whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness

chapters.n: Then sinful actions: their feet rush to shed blood.

f.w: Their feet are swift to shed blood

chapters.n: Ruin and misery follow wherever they go.

f.w: Destruction and misery are in their ways

chapters.n: They have never known the path of peace.

f.w: the way of peace have they not known

chapters.n: The root of it all: they have no reverence for God. Without respect for God, everything else unravels.

f.w: There is no fear of God before their eyes

chapters.n: These scriptures speak to those under the law — the Jews — so that every mouth is silenced and the whole world stands accountable before God.

f.g: Every excuse silenced, as in a courtroom.

chapters.n: No one is made right with God by keeping the law, because the law’s role is to make us aware of sin. A mirror shows the dirt but can’t wash it away.

f.w: by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified
by the law is the knowledge of sin

chapters.n: “But now” — the great turning point. God’s way of making people righteous has been revealed apart from the law, though the law and prophets testified of it.

f.g: A pivotal shift from humanity’s problem to God’s solution.

f.w: witnessed by the law and the prophets

chapters.n: This righteousness comes through faith in Jesus Christ, for all who believe — with no distinction between Jew and Gentile.

f.g: Can mean faith in Christ or the faithfulness of Christ — both are true.

chapters.n: Everyone has sinned and falls short of God’s glory. This is one of the Bible’s best-known verses on the universal need for a Savior.
But we are made right with God freely, as a gift of grace, through the redemption Christ provides. “Redemption” means buying someone out of slavery.

f.g: Release by payment of a ransom.

chapters.n: God set Christ forth as the atoning sacrifice, received through faith in his blood. This showed God’s justice, since he had patiently passed over earlier sins.

f.g: Greek hilastērion — the place or means of atonement; the word for the “mercy seat” on the ark.

chapters.n: God shows he is both just and the one who justifies believers in Jesus. Through Christ, justice is satisfied and mercy is extended — both at once.

f.w: that he might be just, and the justifier

chapters.n: So where is there room for boasting? None at all. Not by a law of works, but by the “law of faith.” We can’t take credit for a gift.

Paul concludes that a person is made right with God by faith, not by the works of the law of Moses. The Joseph Smith Translation reads “by faith alone without the deeds of the law,” keeping the focus on the Mosaic law.

f.w: justified by faith without the deeds of the law

f.g: The works of the law of Moses — rituals like circumcision, not good works in general.

chapters.n: Is God only the God of the Jews? Isn’t he also the God of Gentiles? Yes, of course!

f.w: is he not also of the Gentiles?

chapters.n: Since there is only one God, he justifies Jews and Gentiles in the same way — through faith.
Does faith cancel the law? Not at all! Faith establishes the law — it fulfills the law’s true purpose of pointing to Christ.
Paul turns to Abraham, the revered father of the Jewish people, as his test case. How was Abraham made right with God?
If Abraham had earned righteousness by his works, he could boast — but not before God. The JST clarifies that Paul means the “law of works,” not good works in general.
Scripture says Abraham believed God, and God counted his faith as righteousness. This verse from Genesis is the foundation of Paul’s argument.

f.w: Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness

chapters.n: A worker’s pay isn’t a gift — it’s owed. If salvation were earned, God would be in our debt.
But for one who trusts God — the God who makes the ungodly righteous — that faith is credited as righteousness. Salvation is God’s gift, not our wage.
David also speaks of the happiness of the person whom God counts as righteous apart from works.
Paul quotes David: happy are those whose wrongs are forgiven and whose sins are covered.

f.w: Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven

f.g: Hebrew kaphar, “to cover,” is related to the word for atonement.

chapters.n: Happy is the person whose sin the Lord no longer counts against them.

f.w: Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin

chapters.n: Is this blessing only for the circumcised — the Jews — or for Gentiles too? Remember, Abraham’s faith was counted as righteousness.
When was it counted — before or after his circumcision? Before! Abraham was declared righteous (Genesis 15) years before he was circumcised (Genesis 17).

f.w: Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision

chapters.n: Circumcision was a sign and seal of the righteousness he already had by faith. So Abraham is the father of all believers, even uncircumcised Gentiles.

f.g: A confirming mark, like a wax seal on a document.

f.w: the father of all them that believe

chapters.n: He is also father of the circumcised who don’t just bear the outward sign but walk in Abraham’s footsteps of faith.

f.w: walk in the steps of that faith

chapters.n: God’s promise that Abraham and his descendants would inherit the world came through the righteousness of faith, not through the law — which came 430 years later.
If only law-keepers inherit, then faith is pointless and the promise is canceled.
The law, by defining sin, brings wrath on transgressors. Where there is no law, there is no transgression.

f.w: where no law is, there is no transgression

chapters.n: So the promise comes by faith, as a gift of grace, so it can be guaranteed to all Abraham’s descendants — those under the law and those who share his faith. The JST reads “justified of faith and works, through grace.”

f.w: that it might be by grace

chapters.n: As scripture says, God made Abraham a father of many nations. Abraham trusted the God who gives life to the dead and speaks of things not yet existing as if they already were.

f.w: I have made thee a father of many nations

chapters.n: When all hope seemed gone, Abraham still believed in hope, and so became a father of many nations, as God had said: “So shall thy seed be.”

f.g: Hoped when there was no human reason to hope.

chapters.n: His faith didn’t weaken, though he faced the fact that at about 100 years old his body was as good as dead, and Sarah was past childbearing.
He didn’t waver in unbelief but grew strong in faith, giving glory to God. (Genesis shows Abraham had moments of doubt — but he kept trusting.)

f.g: He did not waver or hesitate.

chapters.n: He was fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised. That is the heart of faith.

f.w: what he had promised, he was able also to perform

chapters.n: That is why his faith was credited to him as righteousness.
These words weren’t written for Abraham’s sake only.
They were written for us too. Righteousness will be credited to us when we believe in God, who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead.

f.w: him that raised up Jesus our Lord from the dead

chapters.n: Jesus was handed over to death for our sins and raised to life so we could be made right with God. His death and resurrection together are the basis of our salvation.
Having been made right with God through faith, we now have peace with him through Jesus Christ. The war between sinful humanity and a holy God is over for those who come to Christ.
Through Christ we have gained access, by faith, into God’s grace, where we now stand. And we rejoice in the hope of sharing God’s glory.

f.g: Entry, introduction — like being admitted into a king’s presence.

f.w: hope of the glory of God

chapters.n: More than that, we can even rejoice in trials, because hardship produces endurance. Paul doesn’t celebrate pain itself, but what God can grow from it.
Endurance produces proven character, and proven character produces hope. Each step builds on the last.

f.g: Proven character — the quality of having been tested and found true.

chapters.n: This hope won’t disappoint us, because God has poured his love into our hearts through the Holy Ghost he has given us.

f.g: Hope doesn’t let us down or leave us embarrassed.

f.w: the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts

chapters.n: When we were powerless to save ourselves, at just the right time, Christ died for the ungodly.
It’s rare for anyone to die even for a righteous person, though someone might dare to die for a truly good person.
But God shows his love for us in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. He didn’t wait for us to become worthy.

f.w: while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us

chapters.n: If we have been made right with God by Christ’s blood, how much more certainly will he save us from the coming judgment!
If God reconciled us when we were his enemies through his Son’s death, how much more will we be saved by his life now that we are reconciled! The living Christ continues to save.

f.g: Restored to friendship; brought back into harmony.

chapters.n: And more, we rejoice in God through Jesus Christ, through whom we have received reconciliation. This is the only place the King James New Testament uses the word “atonement.”

f.g: Greek katallagē — reconciliation; “at-one-ment,” being made one with God again.

chapters.n: Paul now compares Adam and Christ. Through one man, Adam, sin entered the world, and death came with it — spreading to everyone, because all have sinned.

f.w: by one man sin entered into the world

chapters.n: Sin existed in the world before the law of Moses, but sin isn’t charged to an account where there’s no law.

f.w: sin is not imputed when there is no law

chapters.n: Yet death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over people who didn’t sin as Adam did. Adam is a “figure” — a type or foreshadowing — of Christ who was to come.

f.w: the figure of him that was to come
f.g: Greek typos — a pattern or type pointing forward to Christ.

f.w: death reigned from Adam to Moses

chapters.n: But the gift is far greater than the fall. If one man’s offense brought death to many, God’s grace through one man, Jesus Christ, overflows even more abundantly.

f.w: much more the grace of God

chapters.n: The gift also differs in its result: one sin led to condemnation, but the free gift follows many sins and brings justification.
If death reigned through one man’s offense, how much more will those who receive God’s abundant grace and gift of righteousness reign in life through Jesus Christ!
So just as one offense brought condemnation to all, one act of righteousness brings justification and life to all. Latter-day Saints see in this the universal resurrection Christ grants every person.

f.w: the free gift came upon all men

chapters.n: As one man’s disobedience made many sinners, one man’s obedience will make many righteous. Christ succeeded where Adam fell short.
The law came in to make the offense more evident. But where sin increased, grace increased all the more.

f.g: So that sin would be exposed and recognized for what it is.

chapters.n: Just as sin ruled through death, grace now rules through righteousness, leading to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

f.w: grace reign through righteousness unto eternal life

chapters.n: Paul anticipates a misunderstanding: if grace abounds where sin abounds, should we keep sinning so there’s more grace?

f.w: Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?

chapters.n: Absolutely not! We have died to sin — how can we keep living in it? Grace isn’t permission to sin; it’s power to leave sin behind.
Don’t you know that baptism into Christ is baptism into his death? Baptism unites us with what Christ did.
In baptism we are buried with Christ, so that as he was raised by the Father’s glory, we too may walk in a new life. Baptism by immersion beautifully pictures this burial and rising.
If we’ve been united with him in a death like his, we will surely be united with him in a resurrection like his.

f.g: Grown together, united — like a graft joined to a tree.

chapters.n: Our old self was crucified with Christ so that the power of sin over our bodies might be broken and we would no longer be slaves to sin.

f.g: Our former self — who we were before Christ.

f.w: our old man is crucified with him

chapters.n: Someone who has died is freed from sin’s claim. Death settles all debts to the old master.
If we have died with Christ, we believe we will also live with him.

f.w: we shall also live with him

chapters.n: Christ, raised from the dead, will never die again. Death no longer has any power over him.

f.w: death hath no more dominion over him

chapters.n: His death was a once-for-all death to sin; his life now is lived to God.
So count yourselves dead to sin but alive to God in Christ Jesus. Paul invites believers to see themselves as God sees them — and live accordingly.
Don’t let sin rule your mortal body by obeying its cravings.
Don’t offer the parts of your body to sin as tools for wrong. Offer yourselves to God as people brought from death to life, and your bodies as tools for righteousness.

f.g: Parts of the body — hands, eyes, tongue, and so on.

chapters.n: Sin will not be your master, because you are not under the law but under grace. Grace gives power that the law alone never could.

f.w: sin shall not have dominion over you
not under the law, but under grace

chapters.n: So should we sin since we’re under grace and not law? Certainly not!
Whomever you obey, you become their servant — either sin, which leads to death, or obedience, which leads to righteousness. Everyone serves something.

f.w: his servants ye are to whom ye obey

chapters.n: Thank God that although you once were slaves to sin, you have wholeheartedly obeyed the pattern of teaching you received.

f.g: The pattern or mold of teaching — like metal poured into a mold.

chapters.n: Set free from sin, you have become servants of righteousness. Freedom in Christ means a new and better master, not no master at all.
Paul apologizes for using the human image of slavery, given their limitations. Just as you once gave yourselves to impurity and lawlessness, now give yourselves to righteousness leading to holiness.

f.w: I speak after the manner of men
f.g: I’m using a human, everyday analogy.
Sanctification — becoming holy, set apart for God.

chapters.n: When you were slaves to sin, you weren’t controlled by righteousness at all.
What benefit did you get from the things you’re now ashamed of? Their end is death.

f.w: the end of those things is death

chapters.n: But now, freed from sin and serving God, the fruit you gain leads to holiness, and its end is eternal life.
A classic summary: sin pays its wage — death — but God gives a free gift — eternal life through Jesus Christ. Sin earns; God gives.

f.w: the wages of sin is death
the gift of God is eternal life

chapters.n: Paul speaks to readers familiar with the law: a law has authority over a person only as long as that person lives.
His illustration: a married woman is bound by law to her husband while he lives, but if he dies, she is released from that law.
If she marries another while her husband lives, she commits adultery; but after his death she is free to remarry.
Likewise, through Christ’s body you died to the law of Moses, so you can belong to another — the risen Christ — and bear fruit for God. The Church is often pictured as Christ’s bride.

f.w: dead to the law by the body of Christ

chapters.n: When we lived by our fallen nature, sinful passions — provoked by the law — worked in our bodies and produced fruit for death.

f.g: Living by our fallen, natural inclinations.

chapters.n: But now we’re released from the law that held us captive, so we can serve in the new way of the Spirit rather than the old way of the written code.

f.w: newness of spirit, and not in the oldness of the letter

chapters.n: Does that mean the law is sinful? No! But the law made me recognize sin. I wouldn’t have known what coveting was if the law hadn’t said, “You shall not covet.”
Sin used the commandment as an opportunity to stir up every kind of wrong desire in me. Without the law, sin lay dormant. (Think how a “Do not touch” sign can make us want to touch.)
Once I felt alive apart from the law, but when the commandment came, sin sprang to life and I died spiritually. Accountability brings awareness of guilt.

f.w: I was alive without the law once

chapters.n: The very commandment meant to bring life ended up bringing death to me.
Sin seized the opportunity the commandment provided, deceived me, and used it to kill me — echoing the serpent’s deception in Eden.
So the law itself is holy, and the commandment is holy, just, and good. The problem is sin, not God’s law.
Did something good become death to me? No — sin did, using the good commandment to show how utterly sinful sin is.

f.g: Sinful beyond measure; its true nature exposed.

chapters.n: The law is spiritual, but I am fleshly, sold as a slave to sin. The Joseph Smith Translation reframes these verses to describe Paul’s state while under the law and before receiving Christ’s power.
I don’t understand my own actions: what I want to do, I don’t do, and what I hate, I do. Many readers feel deeply seen in this honest description of inner struggle.

f.g: I don’t approve, or don’t understand.

f.w: what I hate, that do I

chapters.n: If I do what I don’t want to do, I’m agreeing that the law is good.
So it’s not really “I” doing it, but sin living in me. Paul describes sin as a hostile power, like an unwelcome tenant.
I know nothing good lives in my fallen nature. I want to do right, but I can’t carry it out on my own.

f.w: to will is present with me
f.g: The desire to do good is there.

chapters.n: The good I want to do, I don’t; the evil I don’t want, I do.
If I do what I don’t want, it’s sin living in me that does it.
I discover a principle at work: whenever I want to do good, evil is right there with me.
Deep within, I delight in God’s law.

f.g: The inner self, mind, and spirit.

f.w: I delight in the law of God

chapters.n: But I see a different law in my body at war with my mind, making me a prisoner of sin. The spirit and the natural body pull in different directions.

f.w: warring against the law of my mind

chapters.n: “O wretched man that I am!” Who will rescue me from this body that is headed for death? Nephi voiced a strikingly similar cry.

f.w: O wretched man that I am

chapters.n: The answer bursts out: Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord! On my own I am divided; Christ is the deliverer — as chapter 8 will celebrate.

f.w: I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord

chapters.n: After chapter 7’s struggle comes this triumphant declaration: there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus and live by the Spirit rather than their fallen nature.

f.w: walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit

chapters.n: The principle of the life-giving Spirit in Christ has freed me from the grip of sin and death. One “law” overpowers the other.

f.w: the law of the Spirit of life
f.g: The governing power of the Holy Spirit that gives life.

chapters.n: The law couldn’t save us because our fallen nature made it weak. So God sent his own Son in a body like ours, as an offering for sin, and condemned sin in that very flesh.

f.w: in the likeness of sinful flesh

f.g: Passed sentence on sin itself, defeating it on its own ground.

chapters.n: He did this so the law’s righteous goal could be fulfilled in us as we live by the Spirit.

f.w: the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us

chapters.n: Those who live by their fallen nature fix their minds on its desires; those who live by the Spirit fix their minds on spiritual things. What we focus on shapes who we become.

f.g: Set their minds on, are preoccupied with.

chapters.n: A mind set on the flesh leads to death; a mind set on the Spirit brings life and peace. Book of Mormon prophets taught the same truth.

f.w: to be carnally minded is death; but to be spiritually minded is life

chapters.n: The fleshly mind is hostile to God; it doesn’t submit to his law and can’t on its own.

f.w: the carnal mind is enmity against God

chapters.n: Those controlled by their fallen nature can’t please God. The Joseph Smith Translation reads “after the flesh,” clarifying that Paul means living for the flesh, not simply having a body.

f.g: JST: “after the flesh” — living by fleshly desires.

chapters.n: But you are not ruled by the flesh but by the Spirit, if God’s Spirit truly lives in you. Anyone without the Spirit of Christ doesn’t belong to him.

f.w: the Spirit of God dwell in you

chapters.n: If Christ is in you, your body is still subject to death because of sin, but your spirit is alive because of righteousness.
And the same Spirit that raised Jesus will also give life to your mortal bodies — a promise of resurrection.

f.w: shall also quicken your mortal bodies

chapters.n: So, brothers and sisters, we owe nothing to our fallen nature — no obligation to live by it.
If you live by the flesh, you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the misdeeds of the body, you will live.

f.w: mortify the deeds of the body

chapters.n: Everyone led by God’s Spirit is a child of God. Following the Spirit is the mark of God’s family.

f.w: led by the Spirit of God

chapters.n: You didn’t receive a spirit that makes you a fearful slave again, but the Spirit of adoption, by which we cry, “Abba, Father!” — the tender Aramaic word a child uses.

f.g: Aramaic for “Father” — the intimate word Jesus used in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36).

chapters.n: The Spirit itself testifies with our spirit that we are God’s children. Latter-day Saints cherish this as a witness of our divine identity.

f.w: we are the children of God

chapters.n: If we’re children, we’re heirs — heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ — if we suffer with him so we may also be glorified with him. Latter-day Saint scripture promises the faithful “all that my Father hath.”

f.w: if so be that we suffer with him

chapters.n: Paul is convinced our present sufferings aren’t even worth comparing to the glory that will be revealed in us.
All creation is eagerly waiting, on tiptoe, for God’s children to be revealed in glory.

f.g: The creation — the whole created world.
Eager longing — literally watching with outstretched neck.

chapters.n: Creation was subjected to frustration and decay — not by its own choice, but by God, with hope in view.
Creation itself will be freed from its slavery to decay and share the glorious freedom of God’s children. Latter-day Saints teach the earth will be renewed and glorified.
We know the whole creation has been groaning together like a woman in labor until now. The pain is real, but it leads to new birth.
We who have the Spirit as a “firstfruits” — a first installment — also groan inwardly as we await our full adoption: the redemption of our bodies in the resurrection.

f.g: The first part of the harvest, a pledge that the rest is coming.

chapters.n: We were saved in hope. But hope that’s already seen isn’t hope — who hopes for what they already have?
If we hope for what we don’t yet see, we wait for it with patient endurance.

f.w: hope for that we see not

chapters.n: The Spirit helps us in our weakness. When we don’t know how to pray as we should, the Spirit pleads for us with groanings too deep for words.

f.w: we know not what we should pray for

chapters.n: God, who searches hearts, knows what the Spirit means, because the Spirit pleads for the saints in harmony with God’s will.
One of scripture’s most comforting promises: God works all things together for good for those who love him and are called according to his purpose.

f.w: all things work together for good to them that love God

chapters.n: Those God foreknew, he also marked out beforehand to become like his Son, so Christ would be the firstborn among many brothers and sisters. Latter-day Saints understand this as premortal foreordination, which still depends on our choices.

f.g: Mark out beforehand; Latter-day Saints speak of foreordination, not a fixed fate.

f.w: conformed to the image of his Son

chapters.n: Those he marked out, he called; those he called, he justified; those he justified, he glorified. Paul sketches God’s plan from premortal life to glory.
What then? If God is for us, who can stand against us? Paul moves into a hymn of confidence.

f.w: If God be for us, who can be against us?

chapters.n: God didn’t spare his own Son but gave him for us all. Won’t he also freely give us everything along with him? The greatest gift guarantees the rest.
Who can bring a charge against God’s chosen ones? It is God himself who declares them righteous.
Who can condemn? Christ died, rose, sits at God’s right hand, and pleads for us. Our Judge is also our Advocate.

f.w: at the right hand of God

chapters.n: Who can separate us from Christ’s love? Hardship, distress, persecution, hunger, poverty, danger, or violent death? Paul had faced nearly all of these.
Paul quotes a psalm: for God’s sake we face death all day long, treated like sheep for slaughter. Suffering for faith is nothing new.

f.w: we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter

chapters.n: No — in all these things we are more than conquerors through the One who loved us. We don’t merely survive trials; we triumph through Christ.
Paul is convinced that nothing — not death or life, angels or ruling powers, present or future —
— nothing high or deep, nothing in all creation, can separate us from God’s love in Christ Jesus our Lord. One of the most reassuring sentences in all scripture.

f.w: the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus

chapters.n: Paul begins a new section (chapters 9–11) about Israel’s place in God’s plan. He solemnly affirms, with the Holy Ghost as witness to his conscience, that he speaks the truth.

f.w: I say the truth in Christ, I lie not

chapters.n: His heart carries deep, unceasing grief — because most of his fellow Jews had not accepted Jesus as the Messiah.
He could almost wish himself cut off from Christ if it would save his own people. Like Moses, Paul loved Israel enough to offer himself for them.

f.g: Greek anathema — devoted to destruction, cut off.

f.w: I could wish that myself were accursed

chapters.n: Paul lists Israel’s great privileges: adoption as God’s children, the glory of his presence, the covenants, the law, temple worship, and the promises.

f.g: The visible presence of God among Israel (the Shekinah).

chapters.n: Theirs are the patriarchs, and from them, by human descent, came the Christ — who is over all, God blessed forever.

f.g: The patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

f.w: of whom as concerning the flesh Christ came

chapters.n: This doesn’t mean God’s word has failed. Not everyone descended from Israel truly belongs to Israel. Covenant identity is about faithfulness, not just ancestry.

f.w: they are not all Israel, which are of Israel

chapters.n: Not all of Abraham’s descendants are his true children. God said the covenant line would come through Isaac — not through Ishmael.

f.w: In Isaac shall thy seed be called

chapters.n: It isn’t physical descent that makes someone God’s child; the children of the promise are counted as true descendants.
The promise was: “At this time next year I will return, and Sarah will have a son.” Isaac’s birth came by God’s word, not human ability.
Another example: Rebekah conceived twins by our father Isaac.
Before the twins were born or had done anything good or bad, God made his choice — so his purpose of election would stand on his calling, not on their works.

f.g: God’s choosing — here, for a role or birthright in his covenant plan.

chapters.n: Rebekah was told, “The elder shall serve the younger.” Esau’s descendants (Edom) would serve Jacob’s (Israel).

f.w: The elder shall serve the younger

chapters.n: Paul quotes Malachi: “Jacob I loved, Esau I hated.” In Hebrew idiom, “hate” can mean “love less” or “not choose.” Malachi speaks of the nations of Israel and Edom.

f.w: Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated

chapters.n: Is God unjust, then? Certainly not!
God told Moses: “I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy.” Mercy is God’s free gift, never something we can demand.

f.w: I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy

chapters.n: So it doesn’t ultimately depend on human desire or effort but on God, who shows mercy. Our choices matter, but salvation itself is God’s gift.

f.g: One who strives, as a runner in a race.

chapters.n: Scripture says God raised Pharaoh up to show His power and spread His name throughout the earth. Even opposition served God’s purposes.

f.w: Even for this same purpose have I raised thee up

chapters.n: So God shows mercy to whom he chooses and hardens whom he chooses. The Joseph Smith Translation of Exodus says Pharaoh hardened his own heart, preserving human agency.
An objection: then why does God still blame anyone? Who can resist his will?
Paul responds: Who are you, a human being, to talk back to God? Should a clay pot ask its maker, “Why did you make me like this?”

f.w: Shall the thing formed say to him that formed it

chapters.n: Doesn’t the potter have the right to make from one lump of clay one vessel for special use and another for ordinary use?

f.w: Hath not the potter power over the clay

chapters.n: What if God, wanting to show his judgment and power, patiently bore with “vessels of wrath” ready for destruction? His long patience leaves room to repent.
And he did it to make known his glorious riches to the “vessels of mercy” he prepared for glory.
That means us — called not only from among the Jews but also from the Gentiles.

f.w: not of the Jews only, but also of the Gentiles

chapters.n: As God said through Hosea: I will call those who were not my people, “my people,” and her who was not loved, “beloved.”

f.w: I will call them my people, which were not my people

chapters.n: In the very place they were told, “You are not my people,” they will be called children of the living God.

f.w: the children of the living God

chapters.n: Isaiah cried out about Israel: even if they are as numerous as the sand of the sea, only a remnant will be saved.
The Lord will carry out his word on the earth fully and swiftly.

f.w: a short work will the Lord make upon the earth

chapters.n: As Isaiah said, if the Lord of hosts hadn’t left us some descendants, we would have been wiped out like Sodom and Gomorrah.

f.g: Hebrew for “hosts” or “armies” — the Lord of heaven’s armies.

f.w: Except the Lord of Sabaoth had left us a seed

chapters.n: What’s the conclusion? Gentiles who weren’t pursuing righteousness have obtained it — the righteousness that comes by faith.

f.w: the righteousness which is of faith

chapters.n: But Israel, pursuing a law that promised righteousness, didn’t reach it.
Why? Because they pursued it through works of the law instead of faith. They stumbled over the “stumbling stone” — Christ.

As Isaiah wrote, God laid in Zion a stone that makes people stumble, a rock that offends — but whoever trusts in him will never be put to shame. Jacob in the Book of Mormon also foresaw Israel stumbling over this stone.

f.w: Behold, I lay in Sion a stumblingstone and rock of offence

f.g: Will not be disappointed or put to shame.

chapters.n: Paul’s deepest longing and prayer is that his fellow Israelites will be saved. His teaching flows from love, not resentment.
He can testify that they are zealous for God — but their zeal isn’t guided by true understanding. Sincerity alone isn’t enough.

f.w: a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge

chapters.n: Not understanding the righteousness God gives, they tried to set up their own, and wouldn’t submit to God’s way.
Christ is the “end” of the law — its goal and fulfillment — bringing righteousness to everyone who believes. The law of Moses pointed to him all along.

f.w: Christ is the end of the law

chapters.n: Moses described law-based righteousness: whoever does these things will live by them. That requires perfect obedience no one can achieve alone.

f.w: the man which doeth those things shall live by them

chapters.n: But faith-based righteousness says: Don’t ask, “Who will go up to heaven?” — as if we had to bring Christ down ourselves. He has already come.
Or, “Who will go down into the deep?” — as if we had to raise Christ from the dead. He has already risen.

f.w: Who shall descend into the deep?

chapters.n: Instead, the message is close to you — in your mouth and in your heart. This is the word of faith we preach. Salvation isn’t far off or impossible to reach.
If you openly declare that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. Faith and testimony go together.

f.w: confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus
God hath raised him from the dead

chapters.n: With the heart we believe and are made righteous; with the mouth we declare our faith and are saved.
Scripture says whoever believes in him will not be put to shame.

f.w: Whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed

chapters.n: There is no distinction between Jew and Greek. The same Lord is Lord of all and generously blesses everyone who calls on him.

f.w: there is no difference between the Jew and the Greek

chapters.n: As Joel prophesied, everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.

f.w: whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved

chapters.n: But how can people call on someone they don’t believe in? How can they believe without hearing? How can they hear without someone preaching? A chain of steps.

f.w: how shall they hear without a preacher?

chapters.n: And how can anyone preach unless they are sent? Isaiah praised the beautiful feet of messengers bringing good news. Authorized sending matters.

f.w: How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace

chapters.n: But not everyone accepted the good news. Isaiah asked, “Lord, who has believed our message?”

f.w: Lord, who hath believed our report?

chapters.n: So faith comes from hearing, and hearing comes through the word of God (many manuscripts read “the word of Christ”). Faith grows as we hear and receive God’s word.
Haven’t they heard? Indeed they have — Paul applies a psalm about creation’s voice to the gospel spreading worldwide.

f.w: their sound went into all the earth

chapters.n: Didn’t Israel understand? Moses foretold that God would make Israel jealous through a “nation that is not a nation” — the Gentiles.

f.w: I will provoke you to jealousy by them that are no people

chapters.n: Isaiah boldly says that God was found by people who weren’t looking for him — the Gentiles.

f.w: I was found of them that sought me not

chapters.n: But to Israel God says: all day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and stubborn people. God’s arms remain open — an image the Book of Mormon repeats often.

f.w: All day long I have stretched forth my hands

chapters.n: Has God rejected his people Israel? Absolutely not! Paul himself is proof — an Israelite, descendant of Abraham, from the tribe of Benjamin, who believes in Christ.

f.w: Hath God cast away his people?

chapters.n: God hasn’t rejected the people he foreknew. Remember Elijah’s complaint against Israel?
Elijah cried, “Lord, they have killed your prophets, torn down your altars; I alone am left, and they want to kill me too.”

f.w: I am left alone, and they seek my life

chapters.n: God answered: I have kept for myself seven thousand who have not bowed to Baal. Elijah was never as alone as he felt.

f.w: I have reserved to myself seven thousand men

f.g: The Canaanite storm god whose worship tempted Israel.

chapters.n: So today, too, there is a faithful remnant, chosen by grace.

f.w: a remnant according to the election of grace

chapters.n: And if it’s by grace, it isn’t based on works — otherwise grace wouldn’t be grace. A gift that must be earned is no longer a gift.

f.w: if by grace, then is it no more of works

chapters.n: So Israel as a whole didn’t obtain what it sought, but the chosen remnant did, and the rest were hardened.
As scripture says, God gave them a spirit of stupor — eyes that don’t see and ears that don’t hear — to this very day.

f.w: eyes that they should not see

chapters.n: David says, Let their table — their feasts and blessings — become a snare and a trap. What should have nourished them became a stumbling point.

f.w: Let their table be made a snare

chapters.n: Let their eyes be darkened and their backs always bent — a picture of spiritual blindness and burden.
Did Israel stumble so as to fall beyond recovery? Never! Through their misstep, salvation came to the Gentiles — to make Israel jealous and draw them back.
If their stumble brought riches to the world, and their loss enriched the Gentiles, imagine the blessing when Israel is fully restored!
Paul speaks to the Gentile believers: as apostle to the Gentiles, he magnifies his calling.
He hopes his success among Gentiles will stir his own people to want the same blessings, and save some of them.

f.g: Jealous desire to have the same.

chapters.n: If their being set aside brought reconciliation to the world, their acceptance will be nothing less than life from the dead!
If the first portion of dough offered to God is holy, so is the whole batch; if the root is holy, so are the branches. The patriarchs’ holiness extends to their descendants.

f.g: The first portion of dough, offered to God (Numbers 15:19-21).
The patriarchs — Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

chapters.n: Paul’s olive tree allegory: some natural branches (Israelites) were broken off, and you Gentiles — wild olive shoots — were grafted in to share the tree’s rich root.
So don’t look down on the natural branches. Remember: you don’t support the root — the root supports you. Gentile Christians owe their blessings to Israel’s covenants.
You might say, “Branches were broken off so I could be grafted in.”
True — they were broken off for unbelief, and you stand only by faith. So don’t be proud; be reverent.

f.g: Don’t be arrogant; stay humble and reverent.

chapters.n: If God didn’t spare the natural branches, he won’t spare you either if you fall into unbelief.
See both the kindness and the severity of God: severity to those who fell, kindness to you — if you continue in his kindness. Otherwise you too will be cut off.

f.w: the goodness and severity of God
if thou continue in his goodness

chapters.n: And Israel, if they don’t persist in unbelief, will be grafted back in — God is able to do it. The door of return stays open.

f.w: God is able to graft them in again

chapters.n: If you, a wild branch, were grafted against nature into a cultivated olive tree, how much more easily will the natural branches be grafted back into their own tree!

Paul reveals a “mystery” — a truth made known by revelation: Israel’s partial hardening will last until the full number of Gentiles has come in. Latter-day Saints see this fulfilled as the gospel goes first to the Gentiles in the last days, then to Israel.

f.g: A sacred truth hidden until revealed by God.

f.w: until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in

chapters.n: And so all Israel will be saved. Isaiah prophesied a Deliverer coming from Zion to turn ungodliness away from Jacob.

f.w: There shall come out of Sion the Deliverer

chapters.n: This is God’s covenant with them: he will take away their sins.

f.w: this is my covenant unto them

chapters.n: Regarding the gospel, they are currently opponents for your benefit; but regarding God’s choice, they are still beloved because of their ancestors.
God’s gifts and his calling are irrevocable — he never takes back his covenant promises.

f.g: Irrevocable; God does not change his mind about them.

f.w: the gifts and calling of God

chapters.n: Just as you Gentiles once disobeyed God but have now received mercy because of Israel’s disobedience,
so Israel has now disobeyed, so that through the mercy shown to you they too may now receive mercy.
God has bound everyone together in disobedience so he could show mercy to all. All need mercy; all are offered it.

f.g: Shut them all up together under disobedience.

f.w: that he might have mercy upon all

chapters.n: Paul bursts into praise: Oh, the depth of God’s riches, wisdom, and knowledge! How unsearchable his judgments and untraceable his ways!
Who has known the Lord’s mind? Who has ever been his adviser?

f.w: who hath known the mind of the Lord?

chapters.n: Who has ever given God something that God must repay? We are always in his debt.

f.w: who hath first given to him

chapters.n: Everything comes from him, exists through him, and returns to him. To him be glory forever. Amen.

f.w: of him, and through him, and to him, are all things

chapters.n: The letter now turns from doctrine to daily living. In light of God’s mercies, Paul urges us to offer our whole selves to God as a “living sacrifice” — not slain on an altar, but consecrated in everyday life.

f.g: Logical, fitting worship — the sensible response to God’s mercy.

chapters.n: Don’t let the world squeeze you into its mold, but be transformed by renewing your mind. Then you can discover and prove what God’s good, pleasing, and perfect will is.

f.w: be not conformed to this world
f.g: Don’t be shaped by the patterns of this age.
Greek metamorphoō — changed in form, like a caterpillar to a butterfly.

chapters.n: By the grace of his calling, Paul tells everyone: don’t think of yourself more highly than you should, but judge yourself soberly, according to the faith God has given you.

f.w: not to think of himself more highly

chapters.n: Just as one body has many parts with different functions,
so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and each of us belongs to all the others. We need each other.
We have different gifts according to the grace given us. If prophecy, use it in proportion to your faith.
If your gift is serving, serve; if teaching, teach.
If encouraging, encourage; if giving, give generously; if leading, lead diligently; if showing mercy, do it cheerfully. How we serve matters as much as whether we serve.
Let love be genuine, not fake. Hate what is evil; hold tightly to what is good.

f.w: cleave to that which is good

chapters.n: Love one another with family affection, and try to outdo each other in showing honor.
Don’t be lazy in your efforts; be on fire spiritually as you serve the Lord.
Rejoice in hope, endure in trouble, and keep praying constantly.
Share with the saints in need, and practice hospitality — eagerly welcoming others.
Bless those who persecute you; bless and don’t curse. Paul echoes Jesus’ Sermon on the Mount.
Celebrate with those who celebrate, and grieve with those who grieve. Empathy is a sign of true discipleship.
Live in harmony. Don’t be proud; associate with humble people. Don’t think you know it all.

f.w: condescend to men of low estate
Be not wise in your own conceits

chapters.n: Don’t repay evil with evil. Be careful to do what everyone recognizes as honorable.

f.w: Recompense to no man evil for evil

chapters.n: As far as it depends on you, live at peace with everyone. Sometimes peace isn’t possible, but don’t let the obstacle be you.
Dear friends, never take revenge. Leave room for God’s justice, for scripture says, “Vengeance is mine; I will repay.”

f.w: Vengeance is mine; I will repay

chapters.n: If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if thirsty, give him a drink. In doing so you heap burning coals on his head — kindness that may bring shame and lead to change of heart.

f.w: if thine enemy hunger, feed him
heap coals of fire on his head
f.g: A proverb, likely meaning to make him burn with remorse.

chapters.n: Don’t be conquered by evil, but conquer evil with good. Good is stronger than evil in the end.

Everyone should respect governing authorities, Paul says, because ultimately all authority exists under God. Christians in Rome lived under Nero’s early, relatively stable years. The JST applies these opening verses to authority in the Church.

f.w: be subject unto the higher powers

chapters.n: So whoever rebels against rightful authority resists what God has established and brings judgment on themselves.
Rulers aren’t a threat to people who do good, but to wrongdoers. Want to live without fear of the authorities? Do good, and you will earn their approval.

f.w: rulers are not a terror to good works

chapters.n: A ruler is God’s servant for your good. But if you do wrong, be afraid — the authorities don’t carry the sword for nothing; they punish evildoers on God’s behalf.

f.w: beareth not the sword in vain
f.g: The sword symbolized a government’s power to punish.

chapters.n: So obey, not only to avoid punishment but because your conscience tells you it’s right.
That’s also why you pay taxes — officials are God’s servants who devote themselves to governing.

f.g: Taxes paid to a ruling power.

chapters.n: Give everyone what you owe them: taxes, revenue, respect, and honor. Jesus taught, “Render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar’s.”

f.w: Render therefore to all their dues

chapters.n: Leave no debt unpaid except the ongoing debt to love one another — a debt we can never fully pay off. Love fulfills the law.

f.w: he that loveth another hath fulfilled the law

chapters.n: The commandments against adultery, murder, theft, false witness, and coveting are all summed up in one: love your neighbor as yourself.

f.w: Thou shalt not commit adultery, Thou shalt not kill
Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself

chapters.n: Love never harms a neighbor. That’s why love fulfills the whole law.

f.w: love is the fulfilling of the law

chapters.n: Understand the times: it’s time to wake up from sleep! Our final salvation is closer now than when we first believed.

f.w: high time to awake out of sleep

chapters.n: The night is nearly over; the day is almost here. So throw off the deeds of darkness and put on the armor of light.
Live decently, as people do in daylight — not in wild partying and drunkenness, sexual immorality and indecency, or quarreling and jealousy.
Instead, clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus Christ, and don’t plan ways to gratify your fleshly desires. Augustine famously turned to Christ after reading this verse.

f.w: put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ
make not provision for the flesh
f.g: Don’t make plans or room for indulging sinful desires.

chapters.n: Welcome those whose faith is still tender, but don’t pull them into arguments over debatable opinions. The Roman church mixed Jewish and Gentile believers with very different customs.

f.g: Having a sensitive conscience about matters like food and holy days.

chapters.n: One person believes they may eat anything; another, with a more scrupulous conscience, eats only vegetables — perhaps to avoid meat that wasn’t kosher or had been offered to idols.
The one who eats freely shouldn’t look down on the one who doesn’t, and the one who abstains shouldn’t judge the one who eats — God has accepted them both.

f.g: Look down on, treat with contempt.

chapters.n: Who are you to judge someone else’s servant? Whether they stand or fall is between them and their Master — and the Lord is able to make them stand.

f.w: Who art thou that judgest another man's servant?

chapters.n: Some consider one day more sacred than others; others treat every day alike. Each should be fully convinced in their own mind. Jewish believers likely still observed feasts and Sabbaths in the old way.
Whoever observes a special day does it for the Lord; whoever eats does it for the Lord, giving thanks to God; whoever abstains does so for the Lord, also giving thanks. Motive matters.
None of us lives only for ourselves, and none of us dies only for ourselves.
If we live, we live for the Lord; if we die, we die for the Lord. Either way, we belong to him.
That’s why Christ died and rose to life again — so he could be Lord of both the dead and the living. Latter-day Saints see in this Christ’s reach to the spirit world.

f.w: Lord both of the dead and living

chapters.n: So why do you judge or despise your fellow believer? We will all stand before God’s judgment seat — not each other’s.
Paul quotes Isaiah: every knee will bow and every tongue will confess to God.

f.w: every knee shall bow to me

chapters.n: So each of us will give an account of ourselves to God.

f.w: every one of us shall give account of himself to God

chapters.n: So stop judging each other. Instead, decide never to put a stumbling block or obstacle in a fellow believer’s path.
Paul, taught by the Lord Jesus, is convinced no food is unclean in itself — but if someone believes it is unclean, then for that person it is.

f.w: there is nothing unclean of itself

chapters.n: If your food choices deeply hurt a fellow believer, you are no longer acting in love. Don’t let your eating destroy someone Christ died for.
Don’t let something you consider good become a source of reproach.
The kingdom of God isn’t about food and drink, but about righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost. Keep the main things the main things.

f.w: righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost

chapters.n: Whoever serves Christ this way pleases God and earns people’s respect.
So let us pursue what makes for peace and what builds each other up.

f.w: follow after the things which make for peace

chapters.n: Don’t tear down God’s work over food. Everything is clean, but it’s wrong to eat something that causes another to stumble.

f.g: In a way that causes another to stumble.

chapters.n: It’s better not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything else that causes a fellow believer to stumble. Love is willing to give up liberties for the sake of others.

f.w: It is good neither to eat flesh, nor to drink wine

chapters.n: Keep your personal convictions on these matters between yourself and God. Blessed is the person who doesn’t condemn themselves by what they approve.

f.w: Hast thou faith? have it to thyself
f.g: Keep your conviction between you and God, without flaunting it.

chapters.n: But whoever has doubts is condemned if they eat, because they aren’t acting from faith — and anything not done from faith is sin. Acting against conscience damages the soul.

f.g: Condemned — here by one’s own conscience.

f.w: whatsoever is not of faith is sin

chapters.n: Those of us who are strong in faith should patiently bear with the scruples of the weak, rather than just pleasing ourselves. Strength is given to serve, not to show off.

f.w: bear the infirmities of the weak

chapters.n: Each of us should please our neighbor for their good, to build them up.
Even Christ didn’t live to please himself. As the psalm says, the insults aimed at God fell on him. He bore what others deserved.

f.w: The reproaches of them that reproached thee fell on me

chapters.n: Everything written in the scriptures long ago was written to teach us, so that through endurance and the encouragement of the scriptures we might have hope.
May God, the source of endurance and encouragement, help you live in harmony with one another as Christ Jesus would want.
Then with one heart and voice you can glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.

f.w: with one mind and one mouth

chapters.n: So welcome one another just as Christ welcomed you, to bring glory to God. Christ’s acceptance of us is the model for how we accept others.
Christ came as a servant to the Jewish people to show God’s faithfulness by fulfilling the promises made to the patriarchs.

f.w: the promises made unto the fathers

chapters.n: He also came so the Gentiles would glorify God for his mercy. Paul strings together scriptures, starting with a psalm: I will praise you among the Gentiles.

f.w: I will confess to thee among the Gentiles

chapters.n: Moses also said: Rejoice, you Gentiles, with his people.

f.w: Rejoice, ye Gentiles, with his people

chapters.n: And the psalm: Praise the Lord, all you nations; let all peoples praise him. Paul cites the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms to show Gentile inclusion was always planned.

f.w: Praise the Lord, all ye Gentiles

chapters.n: Isaiah foretold a “root of Jesse” — a descendant of David’s father — who would rise to rule the nations, and in whom the Gentiles would hope.
A beautiful blessing: May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace as you trust him, so you overflow with hope by the power of the Holy Ghost.
Paul is confident the Roman saints are full of goodness, well-instructed, and able to counsel one another. He compliments before he exhorts.
Still, he has written boldly on some points as a reminder, because of the grace God gave him in his calling.
His calling is to be Christ’s minister to the Gentiles, serving the gospel like a priest, so the Gentiles themselves become an acceptable offering, made holy by the Holy Ghost.

f.g: Here, a priestly servant — Paul uses temple language.

f.w: the offering up of the Gentiles

chapters.n: So in Christ Jesus he has reason to be proud of his work for God — credit belonging to Christ.
He will speak only of what Christ has done through him to lead the Gentiles to obey, by word and deed.
Through miraculous signs and the Spirit’s power, he has fully preached Christ’s gospel from Jerusalem all the way around to Illyricum.

f.g: A Roman province along the Adriatic coast, roughly modern Albania and the former Yugoslavia.

chapters.n: His ambition has been to preach where Christ hadn’t yet been named, so he wouldn’t build on someone else’s foundation. Paul was a pioneer missionary.

f.w: lest I should build upon another man's foundation

chapters.n: As Isaiah wrote: those never told about him will see, and those who never heard will understand.

f.w: To whom he was not spoken of, they shall see

chapters.n: That pioneering work is what has kept him from coming to Rome so far.
But now, with no more new territory in these regions and having longed for years to visit them —

f.w: having no more place in these parts
f.g: No more unreached areas in the eastern Mediterranean.

chapters.n: — he plans to see them on his way to Spain and hopes they will help send him there, after enjoying their company for a while. Whether he ever reached Spain is uncertain.

f.g: The western edge of the known world; some early Christian writers suggest Paul did travel there.
Helped on my journey — supplied and sent off.

chapters.n: But first he must go to Jerusalem to serve the saints there.
The believers of Macedonia and Achaia (Greece) gladly gathered a contribution for the poor among the saints in Jerusalem.

f.w: a certain contribution for the poor saints

chapters.n: They were glad to do it — and they owed it. Since the Gentiles shared in Israel’s spiritual blessings, it’s right that they share material help in return.

f.g: Material, physical things — here money and goods.

chapters.n: Once he has completed this and safely delivered the gift, he will visit them on his way to Spain.

f.g: Officially delivered this collection, secured it to them.

chapters.n: He’s confident that when he comes, he will bring the fullness of Christ’s blessing. He did come — as a prisoner, but still bringing the gospel.

f.w: the fulness of the blessing of the gospel of Christ

chapters.n: Paul pleads with them, by Christ and by the love the Spirit gives, to join him in earnest prayer — to “strive together” with him, like wrestlers or athletes.

f.w: strive together with me in your prayers
f.g: Struggle alongside me — a vigorous, athletic image of prayer.

chapters.n: Pray that he’ll be rescued from unbelievers in Judea and that the Jerusalem saints will accept his gift. His fears were well-founded, as Acts 21 shows.

f.w: delivered from them that do not believe in Judæa

chapters.n: Then, God willing, he can come to them with joy and be refreshed in their company.
Paul closes this section with a blessing: May the God of peace be with you all. Amen.
Paul closes by introducing Phebe, the likely carrier of this letter to Rome. She served the church in Cenchrea, the eastern port of Corinth, where Paul was writing.

f.g: Greek diakonos — one who serves or ministers; the same word behind “deacon.”
A harbor town about seven miles east of Corinth, on the Saronic Gulf.

chapters.n: Paul asks the Roman saints to welcome Phebe as fellow believers should and to help her with whatever she needs. She had generously supported many people, Paul included.

f.g: As is fitting for saints — the way Church members ought to treat one another.
Helper, patron, protector; someone who used her means to support others.

chapters.n: Priscilla and her husband Aquila were tentmakers who had worked and lived with Paul in Corinth and Ephesus. Now back in Rome, they are some of his most trusted partners.
At some point this couple risked their lives to protect Paul. Gentile congregations everywhere were grateful to them for keeping the apostle safe.

f.g: An idiom: they put their own lives on the line, as if offering their necks to the executioner.

chapters.n: Early Christians met in private homes, and a congregation gathered in Priscilla and Aquila’s house. Epaenetus was one of the very first converts in his region.

f.w: the church that is in their house

f.g: Many manuscripts read “Asia”; either way, he was among the first converts there, like the first harvest offered to God.

chapters.n: A woman named Mary had worked hard for the believers. Paul remembers individual service by name, showing how much he valued every disciple’s labor.

f.g: Worked hard, toiled — a word Paul often uses for gospel service.

chapters.n: Andronicus and Junia were fellow Jews who had been imprisoned with Paul. They had joined the Church before Paul’s own conversion and were well respected by the apostles.

f.g: Probably fellow Israelites rather than close family.

chapters.n: Paul sends love to Amplias (Ampliatus), a name common among slaves and freedmen in Rome. In the Lord, social rank made no difference to Paul’s affection.
Urbane (Urbanus) worked alongside Paul in spreading the gospel, and Stachys was another dear friend. The list shows how wide Paul’s network of friendships was.
Apelles had proven faithful through trials. Paul also greets the believers in the household of Aristobulus, which may have included servants of a prominent family.

f.g: Tested and proven genuine, like metal that has passed the refiner’s test.
Some scholars think this was the household of Aristobulus, a grandson of Herod the Great who lived in Rome.

chapters.n: Herodion was a fellow Jew. Paul greets the Christians among the household of Narcissus — likely servants in a large Roman household — specifying those who were believers.

f.g: Only some of the household were Christians; Paul greets those who were.

chapters.n: Tryphena and Tryphosa, perhaps sisters, worked diligently in the Lord’s service, as did a beloved woman named Persis. Many women were key workers in the early Church.
Rufus was a choice disciple, and his mother had cared for Paul like a mother of his own. Some think Rufus was a son of Simon of Cyrene, who carried Jesus’ cross.

f.g: She had treated Paul with a mother’s care.

chapters.n: Paul greets a group of men and the believers who met with them — perhaps another house congregation in Rome.

f.w: the brethren which are with them
f.g: Probably those who worshiped together in one home-based group.

chapters.n: Another circle of believers, including a woman named Julia and Nereus’s sister. Rome’s Church was made up of many small gatherings scattered around the city.

f.g: “Saints” in the New Testament means all baptized members of the Church, not only exceptionally holy people.

chapters.n: A kiss on the cheek was a common greeting of affection in that culture. Paul asks the saints to greet one another with sincere, holy love, and sends greetings from the other congregations.
Paul warns the saints to watch out for people who stir up division and lead others into sin by teaching things contrary to the gospel they were taught — and to keep away from them.

f.g: Watch closely, keep an eye on.

chapters.n: Such people are not serving Christ but their own appetites and interests. With smooth talk and flattery they fool those who are innocent and trusting.

f.g: Their own desires and selfish gain.
The unsuspecting or naive, not the unintelligent.

chapters.n: The Roman saints’ faithfulness was known everywhere, and Paul rejoices over it. Still, he wants them to be wise and skilled at goodness, but innocent and inexperienced in evil.

f.w: wise unto that which is good, and simple concerning evil

chapters.n: Echoing God’s first promise in Eden that the woman’s seed would crush the serpent’s head, Paul assures them that God will soon give them victory over Satan.
Paul’s companions with him in Corinth add their greetings, including young Timothy, his close missionary companion, and several fellow Jews.

f.g: Timothy, Paul’s trusted companion and later the recipient of two letters.

chapters.n: Tertius, the scribe who actually wrote down the letter as Paul dictated it, adds his own greeting. Paul commonly used scribes for his letters.
Gaius was hosting Paul and opened his home to the whole congregation. Erastus, the city treasurer of Corinth, also sends greetings — a sign that the gospel reached people of influence.

f.g: Steward or treasurer of the city.

chapters.n: Paul repeats his blessing of grace. Many early manuscripts lack this verse, but its words match Paul’s usual farewell.

f.w: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ

chapters.n: Paul closes with praise to God, who can make the saints strong and steady. The gospel is the “mystery” — God’s plan once hidden but now openly revealed through Jesus Christ.

f.g: In Paul’s writing, a sacred truth that can only be known by revelation.

chapters.n: That plan is now made known to all nations, and the prophets’ writings confirm it. Its purpose is to bring people to the obedience that flows from faith.
The letter ends with a doxology — a short hymn of praise — giving glory forever to the only wise God through Jesus Christ.
